clinicalPearls: CPVT type 2 is the autosomal recessive form of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, caused by variants in CASQ2 encoding cardiac calsequestrin-2, distinguishing it from the dominant RYR2-related CPVT type 1.
It presents in childhood with exercise- or emotion-induced syncope, seizures or sudden cardiac arrest in a structurally normal heart with a normal resting electrocardiogram.

The signature finding is reproducible bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia provoked by adrenergic stress on exercise testing or catecholamine challenge, typically emerging above a heart rate threshold.
Because inheritance is recessive, parents are usually asymptomatic carriers and consanguinity may be present, whereas an affected child may lack the vertical family history seen in RYR2 disease.
The resting electrocardiogram and echocardiogram are characteristically normal, so a high index of suspicion and provocative testing are needed to avoid misdiagnosis as epilepsy or vasovagal syncope.

Beta-blockade (particularly a non-selective agent) is the cornerstone of treatment, often combined with flecainide; left cardiac sympathetic denervation and an implantable defibrillator are considered in refractory or high-risk cases.

Exercise restriction and avoidance of adrenergic stimulants are important lifestyle measures, and an implantable defibrillator alone can be dangerous because shocks may themselves trigger catecholamine-driven arrhythmic storms.
Genotyping distinguishes CASQ2 (type 2) from RYR2 (type 1) and rarer genes such as TRDN, CALM1-3 and KCNJ2, which informs family screening and recurrence risk counselling.
reference.pathophysiology: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia type 2 is an autosomal recessive inherited arrhythmia syndrome caused by biallelic variants in CASQ2, the gene encoding cardiac calsequestrin-2, the principal calcium-buffering protein within the sarcoplasmic reticulum of cardiomyocytes. Calsequestrin-2 stores calcium in the sarcoplasmic reticulum lumen and, in concert with triadin and junctin, regulates the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RYR2) to ensure that calcium release occurs only appropriately during excitation-contraction coupling. Loss or dysfunction of calsequestrin-2 reduces the luminal calcium buffering and destabilises ryanodine receptor gating, so that under adrenergic stimulation, when sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium loading is increased, there is spontaneous diastolic calcium leak from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This aberrant calcium release generates delayed afterdepolarisations via the sodium-calcium exchanger, which reach threshold and trigger the bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular ectopy and tachycardia that characterise the disorder, all in the setting of a structurally normal heart. Because the defect is unmasked by catecholamines, arrhythmias are precipitated by exercise and emotion, and the recessive mechanism means that heterozygous parents are typically unaffected carriers, contrasting with the dominant RYR2-mediated type 1 disease.
additionalDifferentials: CPVT type 1 (RYR2, autosomal dominant) — the commonest sibling subtype
Calmodulinopathy (CALM1, CALM2, CALM3) presenting with catecholaminergic arrhythmia
Andersen-Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2) with bidirectional ventricular tachycardia
Long QT syndrome, particularly exercise-triggered type 1
Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation and structurally normal heart arrhythmias
Epilepsy or vasovagal syncope mimicking arrhythmic collapse
additionalInvestigations: Exercise stress testing to reproduce bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular ectopy and tachycardia
Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring during daily and stressful activity
Resting 12-lead electrocardiogram (characteristically normal) to exclude long QT and other patterns
Echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance to confirm a structurally normal heart
Catecholamine (adrenergic) provocation testing where exercise testing is not feasible
Molecular genetic testing of CASQ2, with RYR2 and other CPVT genes on the panel
Cascade genetic and clinical screening of relatives, including carrier testing of parents
redFlags: Exercise- or emotion-triggered syncope, seizures or cardiac arrest in a child with a structurally normal heart
Bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia on exertion
Family history of sudden unexplained death, drowning or sudden infant death, or parental consanguinity
Recurrent defibrillator shocks provoking further catecholamine-driven arrhythmia (electrical storm)
Collapse misattributed to epilepsy that recurs despite anticonvulsant therapy
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, beta-blockade often combined with flecainide, and lifestyle modification, arrhythmic events are substantially reduced and prognosis is favourable. Untreated or poorly controlled disease carries a significant risk of sudden cardiac death, and outcomes worsen when diagnosis is delayed or therapy is incomplete.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing exertional collapse as epilepsy or vasovagal syncope and missing the arrhythmic cause
Being falsely reassured by a normal resting electrocardiogram and echocardiogram
Overlooking the recessive inheritance and failing to test asymptomatic parents as carriers
Relying on an implantable defibrillator without adequate beta-blockade, risking shock-triggered electrical storm
Not repeating or optimising exercise testing when initial provocation is inconclusive
references: Consensus guidance on inherited arrhythmia syndromes
management: Non-selective beta-blockade, particularly nadolol, as the cornerstone of therapy to suppress adrenergically triggered arrhythmia
Add flecainide to further suppress calcium-driven ventricular ectopy when beta-blockade is insufficient
Avoidance of strenuous exertion and intense emotional stress as arrhythmic triggers
Left cardiac sympathetic denervation for drug-refractory disease
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for aborted sudden death or recurrent syncope despite optimal drug therapy
Serial exercise and ambulatory monitoring to confirm control and guide treatment
Genetic counselling recognising autosomal recessive inheritance, testing parents as carriers and screening siblings for biallelic CASQ2 variants
Emergency plan with automated external defibrillator access and family resuscitation training
